Lunatick
LOO-nuh-tik
noun
From the Latin lunaticus, “moon-struck,” from luna, “the moon” — the old popular notion being that the falling sickness waxed and waned with the moon. The Authorized Version keeps the received English word of 1611; the Greek is seleniazomai, formed the same way.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lunatick is the Authorized Version’s word for the falling sickness — the affliction that seizes a man and throws him down in convulsions. The English name and the Greek name behind it both carry an old folk-notion, that the fits followed the moon; the word is a description of what men observed, not a doctrine of what caused it. Scripture itself is careful. Matthew lists the sufferers side by side and does not confuse them: “those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them” (Mat 4:24). Devils are one class; lunaticks another; palsied men a third. The Word of God does not say that every convulsion is a devil, nor that no convulsion ever is. In one grievous case it was: a father knelt and cried, “Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water” (Mat 17:15), and the cure was an exorcism — “And Jesus rebuked the devil; and he departed out of him: and the child was cured from that very hour” (Mat 17:18). Mark records the same deliverance with the LORD charging a dumb and deaf spirit to come out and enter no more (Mar 9:25). The doctrine is not moon-lore but dominion: disease obeys Christ, and devils obey Him, and the ruined body and the invaded soul are alike restored at His word.

Webster 1828 Definition

One affected with the falling sickness; in the old usage, one whose fits were thought to follow the changes of the moon.

expand to see more

LUNATICK, affected with the disorder anciently supposed to be influenced by the moon; subject to the falling sickness or to fits of derangement.

From Latin lunaticus, from luna, the moon — a name drawn from an old popular observation, not from a cause.

The Greek seleniazomai (Mat 4:24; 17:15) is formed on selene, the moon, in exactly the same way.

Scripture lists the lunatick apart from the demoniac and the palsied (Mat 4:24).

In Mat 17:15 the affliction was demonic, and Christ cast the devil out.

Key Scripture

Mat 4:24 — "And his fame went throughout all Syria: and they brought unto him all sick people that were taken with divers diseases and torments, and those which were possessed with devils, and those which were lunatick, and those that had the palsy; and he healed them."

Mat 17:15 — "Lord, have mercy on my son: for he is lunatick, and sore vexed: for ofttimes he falleth into the fire, and oft into the water."

Mat 17:18 — "And Jesus rebuked the devil; and he departed out of him: and the child was cured from that very hour."

Mar 9:25 — "When Jesus saw that the people came running together, he rebuked the foul spirit, saying unto him, Thou dumb and deaf spirit, I charge thee, come out of him, and enter no more into him."

Modern Corruption

An old descriptive word now used as an insult; and a modern age that denies devils altogether, having explained the invisible world away.

expand to see more

Two corruptions meet on this word. The first is common cruelty: lunatic has passed out of medicine and into the mouth as a term of contempt, flung at the enemy in an argument. Scripture never uses it so. In the Gospels the lunatick is a son whose father falls at Christ’s feet, an afflicted body carried to mercy; and the church that mocks such a sufferer has forgotten both the compassion of her Lord and the fragility of her own frame. Afflicted image-bearers are to be pitied, borne with, and brought to Christ — never made a jest. The second corruption is the modern materialism that hears Matthew 17 and hurries to assure us that the boy simply had a disease and the first century did not know better. That is unbelief dressed as learning. The evangelist knew the difference; he named devils, lunaticks, and palsied men in one breath as three things, and then reported that this particular affliction was demonic and departed at a rebuke.

Hold both halves and you will hold the truth. Sickness is real, and it is sickness — the body groaning under the curse that came in with Adam, not proof of any special guilt in the sufferer. Devils are real, and they are devils — not a metaphor for what an unenlightened age could not diagnose. Christ’s authority covers the whole field: He healed all manner of disease throughout Syria, and He cast out the spirit that had thrown a boy into the fire and the water since childhood. Neither the physician nor the exorcist is our hope; the LORD Jesus is. And in an age that will not name the devil and an age that once saw him behind every fever, the sober middle is simply the text: bring the afflicted to Christ, ask mercy as that father did, and leave the diagnosis with the One who commands both flesh and fiends.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means “moon-struck,” the old name for the falling sickness — a description, not a cause.

expand to see more

Lunatick — Latin lunaticus, from luna, “the moon.”

The Greek seleniazomai is built the same way, on selene, the moon.

Both names record an old observation of recurring fits, not a doctrine of causes.

Mat 4:24 lists lunaticks apart from the demon-possessed and the palsied.

In Mat 17:15–18 the affliction was demonic and left at Christ’s rebuke.

Usage

"The lunatick of the Gospels is an afflicted sufferer carried to Christ, never a figure of fun."

"Matthew names devils, lunaticks, and palsied men as three things, not one."

"Christ’s dominion reaches disease and devils alike — and the boy was cured that very hour."
